papers.title: The Genetics of Sleep Regulation in Mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for health, yet the mechanisms that generate sleep states and encode the need for sleep are not yet fully understood. Mouse genetics has begun to transform these mechanisms into testable problems by linking specific genes and circuits to vigilance-state dynamics. Here, we review forward-genetic approaches that have uncovered unanticipated regulators as well as reverse-genetic strategies accelerated by CRISPR and adult brain-wide adeno-associated virus (AAV) perturbation. Recent work converges on phosphorylation-centered control of non-rapid-eye-movement sleep (NREMS), exemplified by the SIK3-HDAC4 pathway and related kinase-phosphatase networks. We discuss how neuromodulators orchestrate vigilance states through circuit- and receptor-dependent mechanisms and discuss emerging roles of ion channels, astrocytes, and microglia. Finally, we address methodological constraints in mouse sleep phenotyping and genetic manipulation that shape the interpretation of sleep phenotypes.

papers.title: Propofol rapidly reverses cognitive impairments with restoration of sleep stability and alleviation of neuroinflammation in sleep-deprived mice.
papers.abstract: Acute total sleep deprivation (SD) produces immediate and severe cognitive impairments. Although propofol has been shown to be effective against cognitive impairments under certain SD circumstances, its pharmacological profile under acute total SD remains to be further explored. The present study found that a single subanesthetic bolus of propofol (35-50 mg/kg, i.p.) rapidly ameliorated acute total SD-induced cognitive impairments, with effects observed as early as one hour after administration and persisting for 24 hours in the Y-maze test, whereas the classical hypnotic zolpidem (ZPD, 1.25-5 mg/kg) was ineffective in rescuing cognition. Propofol's cognitive-improving effect was also demonstrated in novel object recognition and object location recognition tasks. Meanwhile, non-invasive sleep monitoring revealed that propofol increased the proportions of medium-to-long duration non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep (64-128 seconds), and reduced the episode numbers of short-duration NREM sleep (0-4, 4-8, and 8-16 seconds) in SD mice. EEG/EMG recordings confirmed that propofol increased total NREM duration by prolonging mean episode duration. In contrast, ZPD failed to reverse NREM sleep fragmentation under either monitoring modality, although it did prolong total NREM sleep duration. Moreover, propofol upregulated the core circadian regulator BMAL1, reduced the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β and TNF-α), restored the expression of key neuroplasticity-related proteins (BDNF, PSD-95, and SYN), and reversed SD-induced loss of dendritic spines in the hippocampus. Together, these findings suggest that propofol rapidly ameliorates SD-induced cognitive impairments, and that this behavioral rescue is associated with the restoration of sleep stability and attenuation of neuroinflammation.

papers.title: Transcranial temporal interference stimulation increases slow waves during human NREM sleep
papers.abstract: Slow waves are a hallmark of sleep homeostasis and a target for enhancing restorative sleep. Transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) can non-invasively deliver a low-frequency envelope to deep targets and has been shown to increase spectral slow-wave activity during sleep. It remains untested whether tTIS also alters discrete slow waves, how their cortical expression changes, and whether the field each brain receives relates to the response. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, 32 participants received 1 Hz tTIS and 11 a carrier-only control in 3-min episodes targeting the left insula/ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Combining high-density electroencephalography (EEG), source reconstruction and individualized field modeling, we found that tTIS increased slow-wave density by about 20% during and 30% after stimulation, across shallow and deep waves, with limited morphology change. The carrier-only control showed no detected density change. In source space, each wave involved more cortex in both arms, while wave origins did not change. A dose-response analysis showed that tTIS participants who received a stronger modeled field shifted further toward N3 sleep during stimulation, a relation not seen in the control. These results support tTIS as a candidate EEG-compatible tool for modulating slow waves and motivate individualized field modeling to interpret its effects.

Source reconstruction and individualized field modeling showed waves involved more cortex without changed origins.

papers.title: Does recovery sleep structure influence cognitive performance in healthy sleep deprived individuals? A scoping review.
papers.abstract: Given the critical role of recovery after sleep loss in many professional settings, this scoping review analysed studies linking the structure of recovery sleep to cognitive restoration in sleep-deprived healthy adults. In accordance with PRISMA guidelines, four electronic databases were searched using keywords covering three concepts: acute sleep deprivation/restriction, neurocognitive performance, and recovery sleep. Eligible studies measured sleep parameters during recovery, from a brief nap to several nights, following total sleep deprivation or sleep restriction, using objective monitoring (actigraphy or polysomnography), and assessed cognition objectively. Paediatric, adolescent and elderly populations were excluded. A total of 31 studies were included, with considerable heterogeneity in design. The main sleep parameters were total sleep time and markers of homeostatic regulation (slow-wave sleep duration and slow-wave activity), and the main cognitive domains were sustained attention and memory. Total sleep time emerged as the most important factor for cognitive recovery after sleep deprivation/restriction, though recovery also depended on recent sleep history. Slow-wave activity and sleep microstructure may explain interindividual differences in restoration. Most associations, however, rely on group-level comparisons rather than interindividual correlations, and the cognitive functions studied remain limited. Further studies should assess correlations between sleep parameters and cognitive recovery and improve reproducibility.

papers.title: Mechanistic insights into state-dependent synchronization of neural activity by weak tACS fields
papers.abstract: Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) biases spike timing with weak electric fields, but how recurrent circuitry and network state shape this response is unclear. We simulated tACS in a detailed cortical column model in two network states of varying coherence, roughly corresponding to REM-like and NREM-like states. Despite weak impacts on network firing rates, stimulation entrained network activity at realistically occurring field strengths. Global entrainment was initiated by direct entrainment of ongoing pyramidal cell activity, which subsequently recruited inhibitory interneurons in a state-dependent manner. The NREM-like network locked more strongly to all tested stimulation frequencies, independent of baseline spectral power, and displayed larger recurrent-connectivity-mediated phase lags. However, recurrent connectivity was not required for, and did not amplify, entrainment, but instead produced an offset in baseline network activity. Our results highlight the impact of network state on the response to tACS, and suggest that meso-scale models of electromagnetic-electrophysiological interactions must look beyond single-cell polarization and baseline oscillations at the stimulation frequency.

papers.title: Evidence for correlated evolution of sleep architecture in chronotype populations of Drosophila melanogaster created by artificial selection
papers.abstract: Chronotypes are circadian variants in timing of a behaviour. In humans, some studies have associated differences in sleep timing and quality with underlying circadian clock driven chronotypes although confounding genetic, environmental and social factors complicate the interpretation of these relationships. Here, we present evidence from artificially selected early and late eclosion chronotype populations of Drosophila melanogaster which suggest that divergence in chronotype can lead to correlated evolution of changes in sleep architecture. We find that early chronotype flies exhibit greater sleep fragmentation and shorter sleep latency during night, whereas late flies showed weaker and less consistent changes in the same direction. These differences were broadly seen for both sexes. We also show that environmental cues like temperature cycles can modulate sleep timing and enhance chronotype differences, while increasing light intensity delayed nighttime sleep timing similarly across chronotypes. Additionally, when sleep was disrupted by mechanical perturbations, late flies could not recover lost sleep to the same degree as early and control in a time-of-day dependent manner. In contrast, following simulated jetlag-induced circadian misalignment, early flies showed a greater increase in daytime sleep after phase advances. Our findings suggest that sleep and circadian traits can coevolve, offering insights into the complex interactions between chronotypes and sleep architecture. These populations provide an evolutionary model to investigate how circadian timing, sleep architecture and homeostatic regulation may be linked.

papers.title: Simultaneous Two-Photon Calcium Imaging, Electroencephalography, and Electromyography with Intracortical Electrical Stimulation in Freely Moving Mice.
papers.abstract: Simultaneously combining cellular-resolution imaging, electrical neuromodulation, and electrophysiological monitoring in freely moving mice requires a mechanically stable chronic implant and precise synchronization across recording systems. This protocol describes an integrated preparation for cortical two-photon calcium imaging, intracortical electrical stimulation, electroencephalography (EEG), and electromyography (EMG) in freely moving, tethered mice. Using the retrosplenial cortex as an example target, the protocol details fabrication and implantation of the cranial window and electrodes, viral delivery, optical field localization, installation of a detachable imaging interface, behavioral habituation, multimodal data acquisition, and stimulation-aligned calcium-signal analysis. The preparation permits repeated optical access over short- and long-term intervals and generates cellular-resolution calcium signals together with concurrent electrophysiological and motor-state measurements. Representative outputs include continuous multimodal session-level recordings, mouse-level population calcium responses, and paired stimulation-off and stimulation-on response measures. The workflow can be adapted to other experimentally accessible cortical targets by modifying the cranial-window location, viral injection coordinates, electrode trajectory, and implant geometry.

papers.title: Sleep as a window into thalamocortical pathology: generative modeling implicates NMDA receptor hypofunction in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.
papers.abstract: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11.2DS) is a strong genetic risk factor for neuropsychiatric conditions, including schizophrenia, yet the underlying synaptic mechanisms remain unclear. Sleep EEG suggests thalamocortical dysfunction, but scalp data alone lack mechanistic resolution. Computational modelling can bridge this gap by inferring receptor-level dynamics from EEG. We applied a conductance-based thalamocortical Dynamic Causal Model (DCM) to sleep-wake EEG from children with 22q11.2DS (n=28) and their neurotypical siblings (n=17), estimating contributions of AMPA, NMDA, GABAA, and GABAB conductances. Building on these estimates, we investigated which receptor systems, if perturbed, could shift circuit dynamics toward sibling patterns. To address this, we implemented in silico pharmacology by systematically scaling receptor-mediated conductances. Increasing NMDA receptor (NMDA-R) efficacy consistently produced the strongest improvements in alignment with sibling spectra (effect size = 0.32 in light NREM, 0.45 in deep NREM), whereas AMPA- or GABA-based manipulations were weaker. The most influential pathways were recurrent NMDA-R excitation among superficial pyramidal cells and NMDA-R excitation from spiny stellates to superficial pyramidal populations. Exploratory regressions linked greater thalamocortical delay during deep sleep to greater sleep problems (β=0.34, pFDR=0.006), and AMPA-mediated excitation of interneurons during wakefulness to anxiety symptoms (β=-0.32, pFDR=0.032). These findings implicate NMDA receptor hypofunction as a key mechanism in 22q11.2DS and suggest it may serve as a treatment target. We further show that DCM-based virtual pharmacology can simulate drug-level interventions, and we are now testing whether NMDA receptor modulation restores network activity in preclinical models (e.g., mouse models of 22q11.2DS).

Findings implicate NMDA receptor hypofunction as a key thalamocortical mechanism and treatment target in 22q11.2DS.

papers.title: Cross-domain competition for memory reactivation resources during sleep
papers.abstract: Targeted Memory Reactivation (TMR) enhances the consolidation of both declarative and procedural memories. As previous research highlights the importance of cross-domain interactions in shaping memory consolidation, we investigated here whether interacting memories from different domains can be co-reactivated by TMR during post-learning sleep, and in turn enhance consolidation. In a fully within-subject design, twenty-four young, healthy participants learned both a motor and an object sequence learning task that were linked or not by a shared ordinal structure. TMR cues associated only with the object task were presented during post-learning non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep which was monitored with electroencephalography (EEG) during a 90-minute nap. We tested whether reactivating object memories would indirectly reactivate the linked motor memory. Behavioral results showed no overall effect of association but indicated that TMR disrupted object memory consolidation without indirectly affecting performance on the linked motor task. Sleep EEG data point to a competition for reactivation resources whereby slow oscillation (SO; 0.5-2 Hz) and spindle activity (12-16 Hz) involved in both memory protection and potentiation during sleep were preferentially allocated to the covert consolidation of the motor trace at the expense of object memory. These findings suggest that cross-domain memories sharing a common learning structure compete for consolidation resources during post-learning sleep.

papers.title: Cycle-based neurostimulation for control of circadian brain network dynamics in human epilepsy
papers.abstract: Biological rhythms modulate symptoms of brain disorders, yet brain stimulation therapies largely overlook the temporal organization of pathological brain states. Harnessing these rhythms could improve therapeutic efficacy. Here, we show that circadian coordination of hippocampal network connectivity is a biomarker of therapeutic response to responsive neurostimulation in epilepsy. Using longitudinal electrocorticography from individuals with bitemporal epilepsy, we find that alignment of circadian connectivity rhythms between the left and right hippocampus predicts seizure reduction. The daily distribution of stimulation also predicts how these rhythms evolve over months. We capture these dynamics using a nonlinear Kuramoto oscillator model and demonstrate that optimizing stimulation timing in silico can improve predicted circadian network alignment. Our findings establish a cycle-based, control-theoretic framework for modelling and potentially reshaping brain network rhythms, offering new opportunities for personalized neurostimulation in epilepsy and other neurological and psychiatric disorders.

papers.title: Integrating convolutional variational autoencoders and the Gaussian mixture model for efficient manifold learning and clustering of spatially preserved EEG topographic maps.
papers.abstract: EEG microstate analysis segments continuous brain activity into brief, quasi-stable topographic configurations whose quantity, duration, and transition dynamics index cognitive state and neuropsychiatric conditions. The standard algorithm, modified k-means (ModKMeans), operates in electrode space. It performs hard partitioning, assigning each data point to exactly one cluster, and provides no learned representation, no generative decoder, and no probabilistic soft assignment. In this research, a Convolutional Variational Deep Embedding model (Conv-VaDE) is designed, a topographic-map adaptation of Variational Deep Embedding (VaDE) that places a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) prior on the latent space of a convolutional variational autoencoder and jointly trains the encoder, decoder, and GMM. Microstate polarity invariance, the property that a topography [Formula: see text] and its sign-inverted counterpart [Formula: see text] index the same underlying configuration, is preserved through three coordinated mechanisms: sign-flip augmentation of the training set, a polarity-invariant reconstruction loss, and an encoder regulariser on the latent embedding. The model is evaluated on a sample of healthy participants ([Formula: see text] healthy adults, eyes-closed) from the LEMON resting-state EEG dataset using a multi-quadrant evaluation framework, with each method assessed in its native frame and cross-method comparisons performed via rank-based Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Conv-VaDE instead offers a focused set of capabilities the standard ModKMeans pipeline does not provide: a learned generative latent manifold (silhouette 0.232 at [Formula: see text], with very narrow cross-subject interquartile-range width [Formula: see text] across the 203 participants, indicating highly reproducible latent geometry), decoded GMM cluster centres inspectable as scalp topographies, probabilistic soft assignment for transitional states, and a generative framework supporting downstream representation analysis. A rank-based meta-criterion over silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, and Davies-Bouldin yields modal [Formula: see text] for Conv-VaDE (39.4%) and [Formula: see text] for ModKMeans (29.6%); [Formula: see text] is adopted to align with the canonical Lehmann A/B/C/D literature. Within the classical cluster-validity register, ModKMeans attains a higher silhouette and 4-5 percentage points higher Global Explained Variance at every K (Wilcoxon, BH-corrected, [Formula: see text]). The two methods occupy distinct positions in the methodological design space, with the cross-method comparison characterising the trade-off between direct electrode-space optimisation and learned generative representation rather than adjudicating method superiority.

papers.title: EEG Source Localization with High-Resolution 40-Tissue Head Models: A Comparative Study with MEG during Photic Driving
papers.abstract: While MEG source localization pipelines often employ head models of one single compartment with homogeneous conductivity, researchers and clinicians use at least 3 different layers in head models for EEG source localization. Recent AI-based segmentation makes it possible to generate individualized head models with 40 high-resolution, non-nested tissues. We present a pipeline that can make use of, and test, these highly realistic models for EEG source localization: with the boundary element fast multipole method (BEM-FMM), we compute transcranial electric stimulation (TES) solutions on the full 40-tissue geometry and use them reciprocally to obtain the EEG leadfields. Out approach runs on a single modest workstation, requiring approximately 4.5 min per EEG channel for a mesh of about one million elements at a relative residual of 1e-4. We applied the pipeline to six participants undergoing intermittent photic stimulation at half their individual alpha peak frequency, comparing 61-channel EEG source localizations from 40-tissue and 5-layer models with each other and with localizations from simultaneously recorded MEG. We further compared noiseless synthetic EEG topographies of the two models across the entire cortex. The two models produced highly consistent EEG source localizations (weighed relative difference below 3%), both in close agreement with the MEG localizations within the visual cortex. The synthetic topographies also agreed closely, with differences scaling approximately linearly with the angle between the source orientations of the two models, underscoring the importance of accurate source normals in fixed-orientation source models. These results establish 40-tissue models as a practical and robust basis for EEG source localization, and open the way to applications where nested geometries cannot represent the anatomy, such as infants or patients with skull defects, injuries, or tumors.

papers.title: Phosphorylation-dependent ATPase activity regulates subunit shuffling dynamics in cyanobacterial circadian clock proteins.
papers.abstract: Protein complexes are essential for cellular functions, with their dynamics increasingly recognized as key regulatory elements. In the cyanobacterial circadian clock, the KaiC hexamer is highly dynamic, undergoing phosphorylation-dependent monomer shuffling that synchronizes individual oscillators. However, the molecular mechanism of monomer shuffling is not fully understood. Here we combine a chromatography-based method with single-molecule fluorescence microscopy to quantify subunit exchange in the hexamerization domain of KaiC (KaiC-CI) and in full-length KaiC. We show that ATPase activity is essential for monomer shuffling. Through quantitative modeling of experimental data, we found that adenosine triphosphate (ATP) hydrolysis at two independent monomer-monomer interfaces disassembles a KaiC-CI hexamer into two oligomers. Two complementary oligomers from two different hexamers can rapidly reform a mixed hexamer. Mechanistically, ATP hydrolysis induces unstable, shuffling-competent states in hexamers, while nucleotide exchange stabilizes them, suppressing shuffling. The balance between these two processes quantitatively explains the relationship between shuffling rate and ATPase activity across KaiC mutants observed in our experiments. Applying this model to full-length KaiC revealed that phosphorylation of the KaiC-CII domain modulates shuffling primarily by affecting the nucleotide exchange rate in the CI domain. This establishes a feedback loop where CII phosphorylation alters CI ATPase activity, which in turn controls subunit exchange to synchronize CII phosphorylation across the KaiC hexamer population. Our findings provide a mechanistic framework linking ATPase-driven subunit exchange to the robustness of circadian clocks, with implications for activation-coupled dynamics in other molecular machines.

papers.title: Effect of Intraindividual Variability in Sleep on Long-Term Memory Encoding in Sleep-Restricted Individuals.
papers.abstract: Greater variability in sleep across nights is generally associated with poorer cognitive outcomes, but some recent evidence suggests that for sleep-restricted individuals, a variable sleep schedule that allows for prophylactic and/or recovery sleep might lessen impairment in some basic cognitive functions compared to a stable schedule. This study examined whether multiple nights of sleep restriction with consistent or variable sleep duration affected declarative memory encoding differently. After two baseline nights of 8-h time-in-bed (TIB), 44 participants (21-26 years, 20 males) underwent five manipulation nights with one of three sleep schedules: 8-h TIB per night (control group), 6-h TIB per night (stable short sleep group) or 8-4-8-4-6 h TIB (variable short sleep group). A picture encoding task was administered after the fifth manipulation night, and memory performance was assessed in a recognition test after two recovery nights of 8-h TIB. Compared to the control group, the variable short sleep group exhibited poorer memory performance, characterised by a greater tendency towards 'unsure' responses for both old and new pictures (p = 0.05; p = 0.09). In contrast, the stable short sleep group did not show significant impairment in memory performance, but instead showed more correct rejections (p = 0.04). These findings suggest that among sleep-restricted individuals whose sleep duration varies substantially across nights, declarative memory may be encoded with reduced strength, thereby increasing response uncertainty at retrieval even after recovery sleep. Minimising sleep variability may optimise declarative memory encoding in sleep-restricted persons. Trial Registration: NCT04731662.

papers.title: Capacity-controlled EEG denoising: diminishing reconstruction returns on semi-synthetic benchmarks and task-dependent downstream utility.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) denoising is often ranked by clean-reference reconstruction metrics, although downstream task performance is less often assessed. We tested capacity effects and when reconstruction fidelity tracks utility.Approach. A depthwise-separable convolutional denoiser spanned 1.05K-40.26K parameters. Capacity was evaluated on semi-synthetic clean-reference benchmarks (EEGDenoiseNet and a mixed-artifact corpus) and by zero-shot reconstruction on brain-computer interface (BCI) Competition IV-2a/IV-2b. Downstream effects and same-condition metric-utility associations used IV-2a motor imagery, with subjects as inferential units (n=9). Further tests used an IV-2b cross-session replication and within-subject paired-recording sleep staging in 75 Sleep-EDF subjects.Main results. In these semi-synthetic reconstruction settings, capacity effects depended on metric and dataset. Electrooculographic (EOG) reconstruction improved from base8 to base16 (correlation-coefficient increment 0.007264, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.005525-0.009002), whereas electromyographic (EMG) correlation coefficient met the selected practical-saturation criterion from base6 to base8. These intervals are conditional on fixed benchmark source pools; a source-level bootstrap left both classifications unchanged. On IV-2a, matched denoising reduced common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis (CSP+LDA) accuracy for EOG (Δ=-0.057, 95% CI -0.087 to -0.029), EMG (-0.102, -0.152 to -0.056), and mixed contamination (-0.099, -0.152 to -0.046); these effects were supported under Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate (BH-FDR) control, not Holm familywise control. ShallowFBCSPNet and EEGConformer showed reductions in several conditions, whereas EEGNet and Deep4Net had no multiplicity-corrected effects. Reconstruction metrics were associated with downstream change in some EMG/mixed conditions but not consistently for EOG. In Sleep-EDF paired-recording validation, denoisers reduced sleep-stage balanced accuracy under synthetic-EOG and unmodified-recording controls; base16 changes were -0.050 and -0.074. IV-2b effects were near-null under the evaluated 01T/02T-to-03T cross-session protocol.Significance. Reconstruction fidelity is informative but not a universal surrogate endpoint. Capacity claims from semi-synthetic benchmarks should distinguish formal practical saturation from diminishing returns, and denoising evaluation should report subject-level effects and transfer controls.

papers.title: Environmental enrichment enhances hepatic oxidative stress and antioxidant defenses without modulating immunometabolic gene expression in adult male mice.
papers.abstract: Environmental enrichment (EE) is a non-pharmacological intervention based on modifications of the housing environment that increase sensory, cognitive, and motor stimulation, and it has been proposed to modulate immunometabolic responses. To investigate the effects of EE on hepatic redox status, oxidative balance, and immunometabolic gene expression in healthy mice. Male C57BL/6 mice were randomly assigned at 45 days of age to a standard environment (SE; n = 7) or an enriched environment (EE; n = 7) for six weeks. The EE group was housed in larger cages containing (tunnels, nesting material, and objects changed weekly). After euthanasia, liver samples were analyzed by spectrophotometric assays for NAD ⁺ /NADH, lipid peroxidation (TBARS), protein carbonylation, antioxidant enzyme activities (SOD, CAT, GST), GSH/GSSG ratio, and total sulfhydryl groups. Hepatic expression of inflammatory, metabolic, and mitochondrial genes was assessed by RT-qPCR (n = 4 per group). EE was associated with lower hepatic NAD⁺ (p = 0.001) and higher NADH (p = 0.006), lower lipid peroxidation (p = 0.004) and protein carbonylation (p = 0.009), and higher antioxidant enzyme activities. The GSH/GSSG ratio (p = 0.04) and sulfhydryl content (p = 0.001) were also higher. No significant changes were observed in the expression of the genes analyzed. Six weeks of EE were associated with changes in hepatic redox status, with lower oxidative damage markers and higher antioxidant defenses, without detectable changes in the expression of the genes analyzed. These findings suggest that short-term EE optimizes hepatic redox balance and antioxidant defenses, while noting that future studies with extended exposure and pathological models will clarify its long-term transcriptional and structural impacts.

papers.title: A post-training quantization framework for EEG-based sleep stage classification.
papers.abstract: Sleep classification models play a crucial role in assessing sleep quality. Although the classification performance of these models has continuously improved in recent years, significant accuracy degradation is commonly observed when quantizing and deploying them on edge devices with limited memory and computational resources. To address this challenge, we propose a posttraining quantization framework for EEG-based sleep stage classification. Specifically, we first identify convolutional and linear layers within the model, then compute layerwise sensitivities based on each layer's input. We dynamically adjust the threshold for each layer based on its sensitivity, using this threshold to detect abnormal weights causing excessive quantization error in that layer. To ensure quantization accuracy, we preserve these abnormal weights at their original precision while compressing the remaining weights to 4 bits. After quantizing each layer, we employ dynamic low-rank compensation to correct quantization errors and further enhance accuracy, addressing information loss during quantization. Experiments on the Sleep-EDF-20, Sleep-EDF-78 and SHHS datasets demonstrate that our method achieves near-lossless compression: the accuracy of the vast majority of sleep classification models drops by less than 1%, while reducing model size by nearly 8 times. This work provides the first general framework for post-training quantization of sleep classification models, offering a new approach for the practical deployment of these models on edge devices.

papers.title: Performance evaluation of smart ring-derived sleep parameters compared with portable electroencephalography in university students.
papers.abstract: Wearable devices enable convenient assessment of sleep in daily life. Smart rings facilitate long-term monitoring; however, their agreement with electroencephalography (EEG)-based sleep assessment remains unclear. We evaluated the performance of the SOXAI RING -derived sleep parameters against those obtained using a portable EEG device. Of 52 university students enrolled, 49 (mean age 19.3 years; 42 females) were included in the final analysis. Participants underwent simultaneous overnight monitoring with the SOXAI RING (SOXAI Co., Ltd.) and portable EEG device (Proassist Co., Ltd.) under habitual home sleeping conditions. Total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), wake after sleep onset (WASO), and sleep stages were compared between devices. Epoch-by-epoch (EBE) analyses were also performed to evaluate sleep-wake and four-stage sleep classification. A strong correlation for TST was observed between devices (ρ = 0.70, p < 0.01). Bland-Altman analysis showed that the SOXAI RING tended to underestimate TST and light sleep, while overestimating WASO and deep sleep. In EBE analysis, the SOXAI RING showed high sensitivity for sleep but low specificity for wake. For four-stage classification, the overall accuracy was 50.0% and Cohen's κ was 0.27. The SOXAI RING showed good performance for estimating TST and may be useful for long-term sleep monitoring under habitual home conditions. However, EBE analysis demonstrated limited performance for wake detection and sleep-stage classification. Sleep-stage estimates and sleep fragmentation metrics should therefore be interpreted cautiously, and further refinement of sleep-staging algorithms is warranted.

papers.title: Liraglutide Realigns Corneal Circadian Output Programs and Ameliorates Ocular Surface Abnormalities Under High-Fat-Diet-Induced Metabolic Stress.
papers.abstract: High-fat diet (HFD)-induced metabolic dysfunction is associated with ocular surface disease, but its effects on corneal circadian organization remain unclear. We investigated HFD-associated corneal circadian remodeling and its modification by liraglutide. Male C57BL/6J mice received normal chow (NC), HFD, or HFD plus liraglutide during an eight-week protocol; liraglutide was administered during the final four weeks. Corneas collected at eight Zeitgeber time points over 24 hours underwent bulk RNA sequencing, rhythmicity, differential-rhythmicity, phase-set, and network analyses. Ocular-surface epithelial, immune, neural, and structural phenotypes were also assessed. HFD increased rhythmic transcripts from 2040 to 3582, delayed mean peak phase from ZT0:46 to ZT7:47, and reduced phase coherence from r = 0.33 to 0.13. In HFD+LIRA corneas, these measures shifted toward NC (2640 transcripts, ZT0:18, r = 0.31). Among 10 examined canonical core-clock genes, only one met the defined significant phase-shift criterion in HFD versus NC, and amplitude distributions did not differ significantly among groups. Liraglutide treatment was also associated with increased epithelial ZO-1 and Occludin signals, greater corneal nerve fiber density, improved mechanical sensitivity, and reduced neutrophil and γδ T-cell accumulation versus HFD alone. HFD broadly remodels corneal circadian output organization while the examined canonical core-clock parameters show comparatively limited changes. Liraglutide shifts multiple temporal features toward the NC pattern and is associated with improved epithelial, immune, neural, and structural ocular-surface phenotypes.

papers.title: 'Therapeutic potential of resveratrol against REM sleep deprivation-induced memory deficits: involvement of hippocampal BDNF and TrkB protein expression.
papers.abstract: Sleep plays a crucial role in the formation and consolidation of memory, as well as in the regulation of memory-related protein expression. Sleep deprivation (SD) has detrimental effects on cognitive function. Resveratrol is a natural polyphenol with reported neuroprotective properties. This study investigated the effects of resveratrol on REM sleep deprivation-induced memory impairment and hippocampal BDNF and TrkB protein expression. Fear conditioning assessed memory, while the multiple-platform apparatus induced rapid eye movement sleep deprivation (REM-SD). Beginning 24 h after training, rats underwent 6 h of REM-SD daily for four consecutive days. Resveratrol (10 or 40 mg/kg) was administered intraperitoneally immediately before or after REM-SD, according to treatment condition. Hippocampal tissue was collected for Western blot analysis of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) protein expression. REM-SD impaired fear-memory performance, as reflected by reduced freezing and increased latency to freezing. Pre-treatment with 40 mg/kg resveratrol attenuated these REM-SD-induced behavioral impairments, whereas post-treatment with both 10 and 40 mg/kg showed protective effects. REM-SD also reduced hippocampal BDNF and TrkB protein expression, and treatment with 40 mg/kg resveratrol attenuated these reductions, restoring protein expression toward control levels. This study provided evidence that resveratrol attenuates REM-SD-induced fear memory impairment, and this effect is associated with the preservation of hippocampal BDNF and TrkB protein expression.

papers.title: Diurnal Variation in Human Breast Milk: Multi-Omic Characterization and Implications for Infant Circadian Development.
papers.abstract: Components of human breast milk exhibit circadian rhythms that may convey maternal chronobiological signals to infants; however, the diurnal patterns of the milk microbiome and metabolome remain poorly characterized. A cross-sectional study was conducted to assess feeding practices and neonatal sleep patterns in 89 mother-infant dyads. Additionally, 40 breast milk samples were collected from 20 lactating women in a separate cohort at both noon and midnight. Melatonin was measured in all 40 milk samples, microbial composition and metabolites in 13 pairs samples were quantified by LC-MS and metagenomic sequencing. In univariate analysis, neonates receiving mixed feeding demonstrated shorter nocturnal sleep compared to those exclusively breastfed; however, these associations were no longer significant after adjustment for delivery mode. A total of 335,651 microbial features were shared between the noon and midnight samples. Differential abundance analysis identified 20 bacterial genera that differed significantly between the two sampling times. The midnight samples exhibited higher relative abundances of Cognataquiflexum, Segnochrobactrum, and Aquabacterium, with both time points enriched in pathways related to lipid and amino acid metabolism. The noon-midnight differences observed suggest potential implications for infant circadian development. The potential role of circadian-matched breastfeeding strategies in infant development requires further investigation.

papers.title: Impact of circadian rhythm disruptions on the emotional brain: gray matter and functional connectivity changes in the amygdala.
papers.abstract: Acute circadian rhythm disruption (ACRD), increasingly prevalent in modern society due to chronic sleep disturbance and irregular sleep-wake patterns, has been linked to emotional dysregulation, including heightened susceptibility to depression and anxiety. Although the amygdala plays a critical role in emotional processing, the direct effects of ACRD on its morphology and function-and how these changes relate to sleep and affective disturbances-remain unclear. In this longitudinal study, healthy participants underwent 15 days of experimentally induced circadian rhythm disruption, which led to sleep and emotional disturbances. Questionnaire-based symptoms of the rhythm disorder restored by the 30-day follow-up. Ultra-high field (7 T) MRI scans were acquired before and after the intervention to assess morphology and functional changes in amygdala gray matter volume (GMV) and functional connectivity (FC). Our findings revealed a significant reduction in GMV within the left amygdala and its subregions-including the centromedial (CM), laterobasal (LB), and superficial (SF) nuclei-following ACRD. In contrast, no significant GMV changes were detected in the right amygdala or its corresponding subregions, suggesting a lateralized effect of ACRD. Moreover, GMV reductions in the left amygdala were significantly correlated with worsening scores on the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Functional connectivity analysis demonstrated a nearly significant decrease in connectivity between the left medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and the left CM amygdala. Crucially, this work is the first to systematically investigate the neurobiological effects of ACRD on amygdala integrity and its implications for emotional regulation.

papers.title: Individual deviation network analysis and rat multiomics profiling link sleep deprivation to depressive-like behavior and microbiome-metabolome remodeling.
papers.abstract: Disturbed sleep and depression are bidirectionally linked, but the peripheral biological pathway converting chronic sleep loss into a depressive phenotype remains poorly defined. We combined a human individual deviation network (IDN) analysis with a rat sleep deprivation model to investigate changes in colonic mucosal morphology and tight junction protein levels, microbiome-metabolome reorganization, and candidate fecal metabolite signatures. An IDN was constructed in 14,769 NHANES adults (2009-2018) using 14 variables spanning sleep, depression, diet-microbiome, glucolipid, and hepato-renal domains. Two-sample Mendelian randomization provided directional annotations. Male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent modified multiple platform sleep deprivation for 18 h/day over 21 days (n = 5/group). Behavioral, intestinal, inflammatory, microbial, and fecal metabolomic endpoints were assessed, and metabolite covariation modules were used to identify behavior-linked Hub metabolites. The IDN identified Sleep × Depression as the dominant deviation axis, with joint amplification extending to the diet-microbiome (dietary index) and metabolic domains. In rats, sleep deprivation reduced sucrose preference and increased forced swim immobility without altering total fluid intake or open field distance. Colonic ZO-1, Occludin, and Claudin-1 decreased while serum TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 increased. Fecal microbiome and metabolome were remodeled. Module M06 was the only FDR-supported behavior-linked module, localizing to docosapentaenoic acid (22:5n-6), FAHFA 38:5, and N-oleoylethanolamine as Hub metabolites. Sleep × Depression emerged as the dominant clinical axis capturing individual heterogeneity beyond group means. In a complementary rat model, chronic sleep deprivation produced depressive-like behavior, inflammation, and microbiome-metabolome remodeling, together with colonic mucosal alterations and reduced tight junction protein expression suggestive of impaired barrier integrity. The M06 hub metabolites are candidate fecal biomarkers and molecules for future mechanistic studies of sleep deprivation-related depression.

papers.title: Implementation of nurse-led frontal electroencephalography for early neurological assessment in patients after cardiac arrest: the FRONT study.
papers.abstract: Continuous electroencephalography (cEEG) is a valuable tool for neurological prognostication after cardiac arrest. However, registration is often delayed by time-consuming electrode placement and limited availability of EEG technicians. This study investigated the implementation of a frontal EEG (fEEG) configuration using 6 self-adhesive electrodes by nurses within 3 h of Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission in patients after cardiac arrest. The FRONT study followed a type 3 hybrid design. Nurses were trained to start an fEEG through a theoretical and practical session and were supported by a Step-by-Step interactive guide. Knowledge, attitude, and practice surveys were completed by nurses at baseline and after each fEEG application. Correct and timely application was measured prospectively in 60 patients. At baseline, the survey response rate was 46% (49/107); after application, it was 68% (41/60). Most nurses (84%) reported having sufficient knowledge of fEEG electrode placement and monitoring. The interactive guide was frequently used (98%) during fEEG initiation; the median application time was 20 min [IQR: 15-25]. All nurses found early fEEG monitoring meaningful; perception improved since implementation (3.98 ± 0.78 vs 4.54 ± 0.51, p < 0.001). During the implementation, an fEEG was applied in 88% of patients (53/60), including 73% (44/60) within 3 h. Electrode placement was confirmed as correct by EEG technicians in all evaluated patients. ICU nurses were able to apply fEEG monitoring with high levels of adoption, acceptability and fidelity following a short, multifaceted training program combined with an interactive guide. Further research is needed to clarify the interpretability, diagnostic performance, prognostic value, and clinical utility of nurse-led fEEG monitoring in post-resuscitation care. Early bedside EEG assessment by trained ICU nurses may facilitate timely neurological evaluation in routine clinical practice.

papers.title: Sea-Level Polysomnography and Periodic Breathing During Acute Normobaric Hypoxia in Healthy Adults: An Exploratory Study.
papers.abstract: Acute exposure to high altitude without prior acclimatization can induce periodic breathing (PB) in healthy individuals, but practical methods for identifying susceptibility before ascent are lacking. This exploratory study examined whether sea-level polysomnography (PSG) findings were associated with PB during acute normobaric hypoxia in healthy individuals. Fifty-four healthy young adults underwent full PSG at sea level and again under normobaric hypoxia after the chamber was set to a nominal simulated altitude of 3500 m; the device-reported oxygen fraction was 13.49% (approximately equivalent to 3300-3350 m under standard-atmosphere oxygen partial-pressure matching). According to hypoxic PSG findings, participants were classified as non-sleep-disordered breathing (non-SDB), SDB without PB, or SDB with PB. Sea-level PSG variables were then compared among groups. During acute normobaric hypoxia, 20 participants remained in the non-SDB group, 23 developed SDB without PB, and 11 developed SDB with PB. At sea level, the oxygen desaturation index (ODI), apnea-hypopnea index, non-rapid eye movement apnea-hypopnea index, average oxygen saturation during non-rapid eye movement sleep, and lowest oxygen saturation differed significantly among groups. In multivariable analysis, sea-level ODI was independently associated with PB during hypoxia. Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed that sea-level ODI had moderate discriminatory ability for PB, with an area under the curve of 0.798 (stratified-bootstrap 95% confidence interval, 0.653-0.920; DeLong P<0.001). At a cutoff of 1.15 events/h, sensitivity was 81.8% and specificity was 79.1%. In this exploratory study, sea-level ODI was associated with PB during acute normobaric hypoxia and may help identify individuals susceptible to hypoxia-related PB. Validation in larger, more sex-balanced cohorts is needed.

papers.title: Preprocessing and feature extraction co-optimization for low-power EEG-based neurodegenerative disease detection: a benchmark on STM32 embedded platforms.
papers.abstract: Early differential diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD) using electroencephalography (EEG) enables low-cost and non-invasive neurological monitoring. This study presents a lightweight TinyML framework for embedded EEG classification on resource-constrained microcontrollers. Twelve preprocessing techniques and six machine learning classifiers were evaluated on two public OpenNeuro datasets containing 88 participants. All pipelines were implemented on STM32 NUCLEO-64 and STM32WB55 platforms using INT8 quantization with CMSIS-NN. Results show that Sparse Decomposition combined with XGBoost achieved the best performance, reaching 94.46% accuracy and 92.1% sensitivity while requiring only 45 KB SRAM and low execution time, demonstrating the feasibility of wearable EEG diagnostic systems.

papers.title: Warmer night-time temperatures are linked to poorer associative memory performance.
papers.abstract: Ambient temperature is emerging as an environmental factor that may influence cognitive performance in ageing populations. This is particularly relevant in Australia, where people live across diverse climatic regions spanning alpine to tropical conditions. We examined daily temperatures and cognitive performance in 1,873 midlife and older adults (1,297 women, mean age 61.0 years) who completed the Creyos online battery (formerly Cambridge Brain Sciences). Twelve tasks assessed memory, visuospatial processing, language, attention, and executive function. Task scores were linked to postcode-level contemporaneous weather data. The scores were analysed in relation to maximum and minimum air and wet-bulb temperatures and postcode- and month-relative temperature percentiles. Regression and distributed-lag models adjusted for age, sex, education, socioeconomic status, and climate zone, with season included for air and wet-bulb measures. Higher minimum, but not maximum, temperature was associated with poorer performance on Paired Associates, a task assessing associative memory. This pattern was observed for air temperature, wet-bulb temperature, and temperature percentile, suggesting poorer memory performance after warmer nights, both in absolute terms and relative to local seasonal norms. Associations were concentrated within a short-term window. Temperature was not significantly associated with performance on any other task, including measures of short-term/working memory, visuospatial processing, language, attention, or executive function. These findings suggest a task-specific association between higher overnight temperature and poorer associative memory performance, rather than a general reduction in cognition. Further studies incorporating personal exposure and sleep measures are needed to clarify whether night-time thermal conditions affect cognitive health in midlife and older populations.

papers.title: Affective responses during five days of dexmedetomidine-assisted cold-sleep for long-duration spaceflight.
papers.abstract: Quasi-torpor, known as "cold-sleep," is an inducible state of metabolic suppression and mild hypothermia proposed to reduce resource demands and psychological stress during long-duration spaceflight. While cold-sleep can reduce metabolic rate, its psychological effects remain unknown. We tested whether affective valence and arousal measured with the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) varied during a five-day dexmedetomidine-assisted cold-sleep protocol, hypothesizing decreased arousal and unchanged valence. We enrolled six healthy volunteers (5 male, 1 female). Five received the cold-sleep intervention, and one served as a control. Participants received an oral dexmedetomidine loading dose followed by an 18-hour subcutaneous infusion with external cooling, then approximately 2 hours of sleep and subsequent cognitive and exercise testing. PANAS was administered daily at hour 23. Positive Affect (PA), Negative Affect (NA), valence (PA-NA), and arousal (PA+NA) were assessed using mixed-effects modeling including the early-withdrawal participant (n = 5). Four participants completed all five days, and one withdrew after Day 3 for reasons unrelated to the study. Mixed-effects modeling showed no significant day effect for valence or arousal (both p = 0.27). PA and NA showed no day-related trends. Two participants completed recovery PANAS assessments, which were equivalent to Day 5. The placebo control qualitatively showed a similar pattern. Across five days of dexmedetomidine-assisted cold-sleep, participants showed no major adverse affective outcome or recovery rebound. These findings support continued evaluation of metabolic suppression strategies for long-duration spaceflight.

papers.title: Condition-associated EEG signatures in N-back tasks: temporal dynamics, classification, and generalization.
papers.abstract: Mental workload (MWL) monitoring with electroencephalography (EEG) is promising for adaptive systems, but practical use requires models that remain reliable across time, tasks, and users with feasible sensor layouts. This study investigated condition-associated EEG signatures in 15 healthy adults performing two complementary N-back paradigms: an N-back level manipulation (N-LEVELS: 1-back, 2-back, 3-back) and a stimulus-pacing manipulation at fixed 2-back (N-SPEED: slow, medium, fast). EEG was recorded using a compact 8-channel setup. Spectral bandpower features, composite workload indices, and N2/P3b ERP markers were analyzed. Linear classifiers were evaluated using within-subject TRAIN → TEST and leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocols, together with analyses of observation duration, time-on-task dynamics, temporal generalization, cross-paradigm transfer, and exploratory ordinal regression. N-LEVELS and N-SPEED produced distinct behavioral and subjective profiles: increasing N-back level was associated with greater task demand, whereas faster N-SPEED conditions showed greater perceived temporal demand and reduced response-time availability. Exploratory locally corrected spectral analyses suggested more frequent beta-band and engagement-index modulation in N-LEVELS and more frequent posterior/parietal alpha suppression and theta/alpha-related modulation in N-SPEED. ERP analyses showed reduced P3b amplitude under higher N-back levels and faster pacing. Classification performance was modest and context-dependent: N-SPEED three-class decoding was more consistent than N-LEVELS, and all three N-SPEED pairwise contrasts survived correction under both WITHIN and LOSO evaluation, whereas in N-LEVELS only the 1-back vs. 3-back contrast survived under LOSO. Post hoc artifact-sensitivity analyses supported the principal P3b findings and largely preserved reference-decoding and alpha time-on-task patterns. After delta-band removal, neither three-class LOSO result nor the N-SPEED slow-vs.-medium and medium-vs.-fast LOSO contrasts survived correction; N-SPEED slow vs. medium under LOSO also did not survive either high-pass variant. Exploratory ordinal regression showed a clearer ordered relationship for N-SPEED than N-LEVELS. Time-on-task analyses revealed selective non-stationarity, mainly progressive alpha build-up, whereas cross-paradigm transfer did not survive corrected inference. These findings indicate that compact EEG recordings contain condition-associated information, but the small sample, deterministic block order, modest decoding performance, and limited cross-paradigm generalization constrain causal attribution and applicability beyond the present protocol.

papers.title: Quality of life impairment in Parkinson's disease with probable REM sleep behavior disorder is primarily linked to fear of falling and anxiety.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is associated with worse quality of life (QoL) in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, it remains unclear whether this relationship is direct or mediated through specific clinical features. We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional study including 468 patients with PD. QoL was assessed using the Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 (PDQ-39). Multivariable linear regression and mediation analyses with bootstrapping were performed to identify determinants of QoL and potential indirect associations between probable RBD (pRBD) and QoL. Patients with pRBD had worse QoL and a more severe clinical profile. Fear of falling and anxiety emerged as the strongest independent determinants of QoL, whereas pRBD was not an independent predictor. Mediation analyses demonstrated that the association between pRBD and QoL was largely indirect, with fear of falling and anxiety accounting for much of the observed relationship. Depression, gait impairment, and voice handicap showed moderate mediation effects, whereas global non-motor burden had a limited contribution. The NMSS mood/cognition domain was not a significant mediator. The association between pRBD and QoL appears to involve specific clinical factors rather than global symptom burden.

papers.title: Natural Antioxidants in Sleep Deprivation: Mechanisms, Therapeutic Potential, and Future Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Sleep Deprivation (SD) is a condition that undermines the body's functional state and is associated with impaired cognition and immunity, dysfunction of the circulatory and metabolic systems, and circadian misalignment. These alterations are accompanied by biologic stress, neuroendocrine imbalance, oxidative stress, and inflammation, affecting both the central nervous system and peripheral organs. Owing to this dual inflammatory and oxidative nature, antioxidant-based interventions have emerged as promising complementary therapeutic approaches. This review summarizes and critically discusses the current evidence on naturally occurring antioxidant compounds and plant extracts with potential protective effects against SD-related pathophysiological alterations, with emphasis on their molecular mechanisms of action and their multifunctional pharmacological properties. Particular attention is given to their antioxidant, antiinflammatory, hypolipidemic, antidiabetic, and cytoprotective activities, as well as their ability to modulate oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling associated with SD. Overall, the available evidence suggests that natural antioxidants may attenuate the deleterious consequences of SD through pleiotropic mechanisms. However, further mechanistic studies and well-designed clinical investigations are required to establish their therapeutic value. In addition to their potential clinical applications, these compounds may provide further insight into the molecular pathways underlying SD pathology and facilitate the development of novel natural therapeutic agents.

papers.title: Adaptation and Validation of the Turkish Version of the Youth Self-Rated Insomnia Scale in an Adolescent Psychiatric Sample.
papers.abstract: Adolescent insomnia is a prevalent and impairing condition linked to emotional, cognitive, and academic difficulties. Despite its clinical significance, there is a lack of brief and psychometrically sound self-report tools available in Turkish. This study aimed to evaluate the validity and reliability of the Turkish version of the Youth Self-Rated Insomnia Scale (YSIS) in an adolescent psychiatric sample. A total of 83 adolescents aged 12-18 years, referred to a university hospital child and adolescent psychiatry clinic and diagnosed with psychiatric disorders based on DSM-5 criteria, were included. Diagnoses were confirmed using the Kiddie-Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age Children-Present and Lifetime Version. Construct validity was examined via exploratory factor analysis with direct oblimin rotation, and reliability was tested through item-total correlations, internal consistency, and test-retest stability (ICC). The YSIS demonstrated excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.884; McDonald's ω = 0.913) and strong test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.89). Factor analysis supported a two-factor structure (sleep quality and sleep maintenance) explaining 71.8% of the variance. Convergent validity was supported by correlations with the Insomnia Severity Index (r = 0.86) and the RCADS-C (r = 0.65). The Turkish version of the YSIS is a brief, reliable, and valid measure for assessing insomnia symptoms in an adolescent psychiatric sample. Its strong psychometric properties and ease of administration make it highly suitable for both clinical practice and research, addressing a critical gap in adolescent sleep assessment tools.

papers.title: Integrating Inflammation, Pathway Modulation, and Circadian Clock Genes: Conventional and Phytochemical Strategies for Safer Osteoporosis Therapy.
papers.abstract: Osteoporosis is a systemic and silent bone disease that destroys bone microarchitecture, thereby increasing the risk of bone fracture, leading to increased morbidity and mortality. Although it is usually considered a structural deficit, bone remodeling is now fundamentally dependent on the circadian clock, osteoblast cells (responsible for the formation of new bone tissues), osteoclast cells (responsible for breaking down bone tissues), and hormonal rhythms, such as cortisol, melatonin, growth hormone, and parathyroid hormones. Current treatment methods for osteoporosis do not fully restore bone quality and cause many side effects. To address these problems, recent studies have suggested that phytomolecules, as promising therapeutic candidates, can be used for treatment. The use of phytomolecules in combination with conventional treatment, in a time-sensitive manner aligned with circadian biology, is expected to be a better treatment for osteoporosis. Disturbances in the sleep-wake cycle or in neurotransmitter homeostasis dysregulate core clock genes (BMAL-1, CLOCK, PER, CRY) in bone cells, causing instability in bone turnover. Osteochronotherapy involves scheduling the intake of conventional drugs and phytochemicals in accordance with the circadian rhythms of bone cells. This chronobiological method aims to achieve the highest therapeutic efficacy and the lowest toxicity, representing an advanced approach to osteoporosis treatment. In vitro studies have shown that bioactive agents, mainly resveratrol, icariin, genistein, quercetin, and baicalein, have osteoprotective activities with multimodal actions, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and direct effects on RANKL/OPG, AMPK/SIRT1, ESR, NF-κB, and Wnt/β-catenin. The study highlights the importance of incorporating circadian biology into osteoporosis management. The synchronization of therapies with the biological clock can maximize efficiency, reduce adverse effects, and help develop a new approach to bone health. The results emphasize the importance of using phytochemicals as an adjunct therapy, shed light on knowledge gaps in bone remodeling, and suggest possible avenues for utilizing circadian regulation of osteoblasts and osteoclasts to enhance bone density. Furthermore, the incorporation of natural compounds with chronotherapy represents a paradigm shift toward more personalized, safer, and biologically harmonized strategies for osteoporosis therapy. These insights also highlight critical knowledge gaps in bone remodeling research, encouraging future studies to explore how circadian rhythms and neurotransmitter pathways can be leveraged to advance precision medicine in skeletal health. It is now evident that circadian rhythm serves as an important mediator for the maintenance of healthy bones because of its function in bone remodeling. In future research, emphasis must also be placed on exploring the possible differential regulation of osteoclasts and osteoblasts by various circadian rhythms and how such regulation can help enhance bone strength. The review concludes by examining the interplay among neurotransmitter pathways, circadian biology, and sleep quality in relation to conventional and phytochemical interventions.

papers.title: Obstructive sleep apnea may exacerbate periodontitis via microbial dysbiosis: A preliminary translational exploratory study.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is characterized by recurrent airway obstruction and could lead to chronic intermittent hypoxia (CIH). Its relationship with periodontitis and underlying biological mechanisms, however, remains unclear. This translational human observation and experimental animal study aims (1) to investigate whether OSA exacerbates periodontitis and (2) to explore potential microbial and metabolic mechanisms. In the clinical component, patients with stage II periodontitis were allocated into two groups: periodontitis without OSA (N-OSA + P) and periodontitis with OSA (OSA + P). Gingival crevicular fluid (GCF) was analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. In the experimental study, eight male Wistar rats with ligature-induced periodontitis (P) were randomly assigned to normoxia or CIH exposure. Micro-CT, histological staining, ELISA, and qRT-PCR were performed to assess alveolar bone loss and inflammation responses. Demographic parameters were comparable between clinical groups. The OSA + P group exhibited higher microbial richness and a distinct subgingival community structure, characterized by enrichment of Porphyromonas gingivalis and Fusobacterium. 21 endogenous differential metabolites were identified, primarily related to glycerophospholipid metabolism, with significant microbe-metabolite correlations observed. In the animal model, CIH exposure was associated with increased alveolar bone loss, enhanced inflammatory marker expression, and altered microbial community structure compared with normoxic controls. The presence of sleep breathing disturbances, such as OSA, seems to exacerbate periodontitis most likely by CIH, which leads to microbial dysbiosis, and metabolic reprogramming within the periodontal microenvironment.

papers.title: Longitudinal ACC Alterations with Low-Dose Pregabalin in pBMS.
papers.abstract: Primary burning mouth syndrome (pBMS) is a chronic orofacial pain disorder in which the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) serves as a core node in descending pain modulation and central sensitization. Multiparametric MRI evidence for structural, metabolic, and functional abnormalities across ACC subregions remains limited. This single-arm, prospective longitudinal study characterized ACC subregional alterations in 38 patients with moderate-to-severe pBMS and 31 matched healthy controls. All patients received a standardized 4-wk low-dose pregabalin course, with clinical and neuroimaging measures reassessed posttreatment; 30 of 34 patients who completed the trial provided posttreatment MRI data. At baseline, pBMS patients exhibited elevated ACC Glx/Cr (median 2.51 vs 1.93, P = 0.021) and tNAA/Cr (median 1.97 vs 1.72, P = 0.050) ratios, reduced gray matter volume in the left medial superior frontal gyrus and left frontal pole, and decreased pregenual ACC (pgACC) and subgenual ACC (sgACC)-centered connectivity involving the left middle frontal gyrus and left inferior parietal lobule. Glx/Cr correlated positively with visual analog scale (VAS) scores and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores, and tNAA/Cr correlated negatively with VAS and Central Sensitization Inventory scores. After treatment, the mean VAS reduction was 3.28 points (intention to treat; ITT); 44.74% (ITT, n = 38) and 50.00% (per-protocol, n = 34) attained ≥50% pain relief. The median ACC Glx/Cr decreased from 2.51 to 1.85 (P = 0.008) and pgACC-centered functional connectivity increased, whereas regional gray matter volume-including the pre-existing deficits in the left medial superior frontal gyrus and left frontal pole-showed no significant longitudinal change. In conclusion, pBMS is characterized by metabolic and functional neuroimaging alterations within pgACC and sgACC that covary with symptomatic improvement under low-dose pregabalin, whereas structural deficits remain unchanged in the short term. These exploratory findings support the potential benefits of low-dose pregabalin and highlight pgACC and sgACC as promising regions of interest for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: The potential mediating role of social frailty in the associations of cognitive function, sleep duration, and life satisfaction with depressive symptoms in older adults: a cross-sectional study using CHARLS data.
papers.abstract: To examine the direct and indirect associations of cognitive function, life satisfaction, and sleep duration with depressive symptoms, with social frailty as a potential mediator, among older adults. Cross-sectional data from Wave 5 (2020) of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS; N = 4,491; aged ≥ 60 years) were analysed. Depression was measured using the CESD-10, cognitive function using a composite score (orientation, memory, and executive function), and social frailty as a sum of loneliness and social isolation scores. Hierarchical regression and structural equation modelling were conducted. The mean depression score was 16.97 (SD = 5.78). In hierarchical regression showed that life satisfaction (β = -0.265), cognitive function (β = -0.257), sleep duration (β = -0.174), health status (β = -0.156), social frailty (β = 0.113), and self-rated memory (β = -0.073) were significantly associated with depression symptoms, collectively accounting for 28.7% of variance. Path analysis further showed statistically significant indirect associations through social frailty linking life satisfaction, cognitive function, and sleep duration to depressive symptoms. These findings suggest a complex interplay among life satisfaction, social frailty, sleep duration, cognitive function, and depressive symptoms in older adults. Social frailty may serve as a potential intermediary pathway linking these factors to depression. As the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, longitudinal studies are needed to confirm directionality and evaluate whether interventions targeting social frailty can reduce depressive symptoms in ageing populations.

papers.title: Pathological mechanisms of the "lifestyle-immunometabolic-neuroendocrine" crosstalk network in ectopic fat deposition and skeletal muscle decline.
papers.abstract: Chronic low-grade systemic inflammation serves as a pivotal pathological link coupling unhealthy lifestyles with malignant remodeling of body composition. This review systematically constructs and elucidates the molecular mechanisms and pathological progression of the "lifestyle-immunometabolic-neuroendocrine" crosstalk network in ectopic fat deposition and skeletal muscle decline. Upstream multidimensional lifestyle stressors-including unhealthy diets, sleep deprivation, psychological stress, and sedentary behavior-disrupt the gut barrier, endocrine barriers, and mechanical contractile strain, thereby initiating immunometabolic reprogramming and triggering systemic chronic low-grade sterile inflammation. Acting as a core pathological driver, this low-grade inflammation impairs lipid and protein homeostasis, propels lipotoxic spillover and intramyocellular fat infiltration, and ultimately leads to the progressive decline of skeletal muscle mass and function. Concurrently, age-related neuroendocrine axis decline and dwindling sex hormone levels function as endogenous amplifiers, synergistically accelerating tissue microenvironmental remodeling and body composition imbalance in a distinctly dimorphic manner (e.g., postmenopausal estrogen deficiency accelerates muscle deterioration by inducing autophagy dysfunction in muscle stem cells). A deep mechanistic parsing of the regulatory nodes within this multidimensional network provides substantial academic value for deciphering the onset and progression of lifestyle-driven chronic inflammatory disorders.

papers.title: Interrater agreement of seizure onset and spread in scalp EEG
papers.abstract: Objective. Faster seizure spread on intracranial EEG has been linked to worse surgical outcome. If contralateral spread on scalp EEG carried similar prognostic information, it could identify poor resection candidates before intracranial monitoring and direct them toward neuromodulation sooner. Testing this first requires that experts reliably annotate spread on scalp EEG. The interrater agreement for seizure spread detection on scalp EEG is unknown; prior scalp EEG reliability studies have focused mainly on seizure detection. We quantified expert agreement on the laterality, channels, and timing of seizure onset and contralateral spread. Methods. We retrospectively analyzed 79 seizures from 48 patients undergoing presurgical evaluation at a single center. Three board certified epileptologists independently marked the time and channels of onset and contralateral spread for each seizure. We measured agreement on onset laterality and spread presence with Gwet k, channels with Cohen k, and timing with the median absolute deviation (MAD). Interrater and majority vote consensus agreement were estimated with patient-clustered CIs. Results. Onset laterality showed substantial interrater agreement (Gwet k = 0.73, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.83); most disagreement involved bilateral onsets. Contralateral spread agreement was comparable (0.63, 0.48 to 0.76). Channel level agreement was higher for onset (inter rater Cohen k = 0.57) than for spread (0.38). Onset timing was highly consistent (median MAD 0.40 s); spread timing agreement was also high (1.99 s), but less so than onset timing (sign rank p < 0.001). Agreement did not differ across annotators or between temporal and non-temporal epilepsy. Significance. Epileptologists generally agree on onset laterality and whether and when seizures spread contralaterally, although spread channels are identified less reliably. These findings support the feasibility of measuring scalp EEG spread as a candidate noninvasive marker of seizure network extent. The public annotated dataset provides a multi-expert reference standard for developing automated spread detection algorithms.

papers.title: Evidence appraisal of clinical practice guidelines for managing menopausal symptoms: a systematic literature review.
papers.abstract: Symptoms associated with menopause can significantly impair quality of life. Although menopausal hormone therapy remains a well-established and highly effective intervention, a wide range of nonhormone therapies are available on and off-label as options for women in whom menopausal hormone therapy is contraindicated or not preferred. Although multiple clinical guidelines address the use of menopausal hormone therapy and nonhormone therapy for managing symptoms of menopause, the consistency of the recommendations and the robustness of the supporting evidence remain uncertain. Evaluate current United States menopause treatment guidelines in the context of emerging therapies (menopausal hormone therapy and nonhormone therapy) and evolving clinical practice. We systematically searched PubMed and EMBASE for United States menopause treatment guidelines published between 2014 and 2024. We included clinical practice guidelines and consensus statements, excluding those limited to surgically induced menopause. We extracted data using the Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes, Recommendation framework and assessed guideline quality. Of 655 records screened, 13 met the inclusion criteria from organizations including the American Association of Clinical Endocrinology, The Menopause Society, and the Endocrine Society. Guidelines evaluated menopausal hormone therapy for managing vasomotor symptoms, genitourinary syndrome, premature ovarian insufficiency, hypoactive sexual desire disorder, sleep disturbances, and depression, contingent on individual risk profiles. Nonhormone therapies, including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, gabapentin, and fezolinetant, were supported by moderate to high-quality evidence. Most guidelines advise against over-the-counter or alternative treatments due to limited data. No guideline provided decision-support tools or therapeutic sequencing algorithms for nonhormone therapy selection. Seven guidelines were of moderate quality, four low-moderate, and two low quality with none rated high quality, primarily due to gaps in stakeholder involvement and applicability. This review highlights variable quality and consistency in United States clinical recommendations for vasomotor symptoms. Future guidelines should incorporate structured decision frameworks to guide therapy selection based on contraindications, patient preferences, and risk profiles.

papers.title: Filgotinib Safety Profile: A Pharmacovigilance Study Using Data from the VigiBase and Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System.
papers.abstract: Although filgotinib was approved in Europe and Japan, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) withheld approval owing to concerns about testicular toxicity. To address this gap, we conducted a pharmacovigilance study of filgotinib-related adverse drug reactions (ADRs). This study evaluated the safety profile of filgotinib using data from the VigiBase and FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) databases from the first quarter (Q1) of 2017 to Q1 2025. Signal detection involved calculating four disproportionality measures: the proportional reporting ratio (PRR), reporting odds ratio (ROR), information component (IC), and empirical Bayes geometric mean (EBGM), using predefined quantitative thresholds. Signals were refined using OpenVigil 2.1 to account for concomitant medications. The signals were ordered according to their IC025 values rather than PRR value. Analysis of VigiBase data (2207 reports) revealed a predominance of ADRs among female patients (74.8%) and individuals aged 45-64 years (38.1%). Notably, 95% of reports originated in Europe. Strong disproportionate reporting signals were identified for lower respiratory tract infection (PRR = 20.5 [χ2 = 1002.3], lower bound [LB] ROR = 16, IC025 = 3.7, EBGM05 = 15.6) and hypercholesterolemia (PRR = 29.8 [χ2 = 611.9], LB ROR = 19.8, IC025 = 3.5, EBGM05 = 19.5). Time-to-onset analysis revealed diverse onset times (median, 1 month), with most ADRs assessed as possibly related to filgotinib. In FAERS (190 reports), disproportionate reporting signals were observed for epididymitis (PRR = 1060.3 [χ2 = 8350.6], LB ROR = 544.1, IC025 = 2.9, EBGM05 = 512.0) and sleep apnea syndrome (PRR = 62.7 [χ2 = 486.0], LB ROR = 32.3, IC025 = 2.6, EBGM05 = 30.8). This pharmacovigilance study identified several disproportionality signals, including epididymitis, sleep apnea syndrome, infections, and metabolic abnormalities, warranting continued clinical vigilance and further investigation of the safety profile of filgotinib.
